name: Waytemore Castle
text: Your train passes near Waytemore Castle, on the train's {side}, begun as a motte and bailey castle in the time of William the Conqueror, with a great tower added on the mound in the 12th century. It was used as a prison in the 17th century; today only earthworks, the large motte and the foundations of a square tower can be seen.

name: Thorley Wash
text: Your train passes Thorley Wash, on the train's {side}, once a flood pound for the Stort Navigation, which was decommissioned in 2004 and returned to a more natural state. It is home to the endangered Desmoulin's whorl snail, and its dangerously deep silt keeps visitors to the footpaths.

name: Gibberd Garden
text: Your train passes near the Gibberd Garden, on the train's {side}, made by Sir Frederick Gibberd, the planner of Harlow New Town, and his wife Patricia. From 1972 until his death in 1984 they filled it with sculptures, ceramic pots and architectural salvage.

name: Stort Navigation
text: Your train runs beside the Stort Navigation, on the train's {side}, the canalised River Stort. It was built for Bishop's Stortford's growing malt trade and opened on October 24th 1769, with 15 locks down to the River Lea.

name: Hunsdon Mead
text: Your train passes near Hunsdon Mead, on the train's {side}, a meadow between the River Stort and the Stort Navigation that floods in winter. Partly in Essex and partly in Hertfordshire, it is registered common land, with uncommon plants such as green-winged orchids and quaking grass.

name: Rye House Power Station
text: Your train passes Rye House Power Station, on the train's {side}, a gas-fired station fully commissioned in 1993 on the site of a coal-fired station of 1951. It has the largest air-cooled condenser in Europe, and its output is enough for the daily power needs of nearly a million people.

name: St Augustine's Church, Broxbourne
text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Church, Broxbourne, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church opposite the New River. It was built by 1460, paid for by Sir John Say, whose tomb lies south of the chancel, and it has a memorial to John Loudon McAdam.

name: Waltham Common Lock
text: Your train passes near Waltham Common Lock, on the train's {side}, lock number 10 on the River Lee Navigation. At its tail is the Powdermill Cut, dug in 1806 to link the Royal Gunpowder Mills at Waltham Abbey directly to what was then a new navigation.

name: Theobalds Palace
text: Your train passes near the site of Theobalds Palace, on the train's {side}, a grand house built between 1564 and 1585 for Lord Burghley, Queen Elizabeth I's senior councillor. It became a royal palace under James I, who died there in 1625, and was demolished as a result of the Civil War; its site is now Cedars Park.

name: Lee Valley White Water Centre
text: Your train passes near the Lee Valley White Water Centre, on the train's {side}, built for the canoe slalom events of the London 2012 Olympic Games. Opened in December 2010, it was the first newly built Olympic venue to be finished, and in 2015 it hosted the Canoe Slalom World Championships.

name: Rye House
text: Your train passes near Rye House, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house licensed in 1443 for Sir Andrew Ogard, a Danish soldier, and built with more than 50 types of moulded brick. Only its Grade I gatehouse survives; the house gave its name to the Rye House Plot of 1683, an alleged plan to kill Charles II and his brother James.

name: Rye Meads
text: Your train passes near Rye Meads, on the train's {side}, part of the Lea Valley's internationally important wetlands. Its nature reserve has ten birdwatching hides, and one half of it, an ancient flood meadow, is grazed by ponies and water buffalo.

name: Amwell Quarry
text: Your train passes Amwell Quarry, on the train's {side}, a former gravel pit turned into a wetland nature reserve with two lakes. It is Britain's most important site for dragonflies, and a quarter of all British species of molluscs are found there.

name: Scott's Grotto
text: Your train passes near Scott's Grotto, on the train's {side}, which with six chambers is the most extensive shell grotto in the United Kingdom. Dug into a chalk hillside and decorated with shells, flints, fossils and coloured glass, it was completed by the 18th-century Quaker poet John Scott.

name: Stansted Mountfitchet Windmill
text: Your train passes near Stansted Mountfitchet Windmill, on the train's {side}, a tower mill built in 1787 that last worked commercially in 1910, crushing oats. It has been restored and can still turn in the wind.

name: London Stansted Airport
text: Your train passes London Stansted Airport, on the train's {side}, built by American engineer battalions between 1942 and 1943 as RAF Stansted Mountfitchet and turned over to civil use in the late 1940s. It is now the largest base of the low-cost airline Ryanair.

name: David Parr House
text: Your train passes near the David Parr House, on the train's {side}, a terraced house off Mill Road that the working-class decorative artist David Parr decorated in the Arts and Crafts style between 1886 and 1926. Kept as he left it by his widow and later his granddaughter, it opened to the public in 2019.

name: Leper Chapel
text: Your train passes the Leper Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in about 1125 for a leper hospital outside Cambridge. In 1199 King John allowed it a fair to raise money; held on Stourbridge Common behind the chapel, Stourbridge Fair grew into the largest medieval fair in Europe.

name: Waterbeach Abbey
text: Your train passes near the site of Waterbeach Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1294 by nuns of the Second Order of St Francis who had come from Longchamp Abbey in France. The abbey was prone to flooding, and by 1351 the nuns had moved to nearby Denny Abbey.

name: Little Thetford
text: Your train passes Little Thetford, on the train's {side}, a village on a clay island in the fens. A Bronze Age causeway linked it to nearby Barway, and digging before new building in 1995 found a Romano-British farm and a large tile kiln.

name: Ely Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Ely Cathedral, on the train's {side}, which traces its origin to an abbey founded in 672 by St Etheldreda. The earliest parts of the present building date from 1083, and its central octagonal tower and lantern, with the West Tower, dominate the landscape around.

name: Fenland Hall
text: Your train passes near Fenland Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1908 and 1909 as County Hall for the Isle of Ely County Council, which chose March as the more central place in the Isle, with better railway connections. It is now the headquarters of Fenland District Council.

name: March depot
text: Your train passes near March depot, on the train's {side}, built by the Great Eastern Railway in the 1880s close to the Whitemoor marshalling yard. Despite its rural setting, in the 1970s it held about as many locomotives as the larger Toton depot and was the main diesel depot for East Anglia.

name: Ely Pits and Meadows
text: Your train passes near Ely Pits and Meadows, on the train's {side}, old clay and beet pits beside the River Great Ouse that have yielded fossil reptiles about 155 million years old. Bitterns, which are nationally rare, breed and spend the winter there.

name: Queen Adelaide
text: Your train passes Queen Adelaide, on the train's {side}, a hamlet named after its pub, which was named after Queen Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. It grew up only in the 19th century, when the railways reached Ely, and three railway lines cross its main street, each by a level crossing of its own.

name: Prickwillow Museum
text: Your train passes near Prickwillow Museum, on the train's {side}, housed in the old pumping station of a fen village. It tells the story of draining the Fens, with a major collection of large diesel pumping engines, all restored to working order.

name: Hawk Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Great Ouse on Hawk Bridge, half a mile east of Ely Dock Junction. The bridge was rebuilt in 2007, following the derailment of a freight train.

name: The Boat Race 2021
text: Your train passes near the stretch of the River Great Ouse, on the train's {side}, where the Boat Race was rowed on April 4th 2021, moved from the Thames because of the pandemic and the closure of Hammersmith Bridge. Cambridge won both the men's and the women's races; the only earlier race here was an unofficial wartime one in 1944.

name: Denver Windmill
text: Your train passes near Denver Windmill, on the train's {side}, a tower mill built in 1835 for John Porter, whose initials and the year are on its datestone. A steam mill was added beside it by 1863, and the windmill's centenary was celebrated with a supper in January 1936.

name: Stowbridge
text: Your train passes Stowbridge, on the train's {side}, a village where the River Great Ouse, the Relief Channel and the railway all run through the middle. In about 1181 a group of hermit women from Lynn settled in this "desolate and marshy place", in a community that became Crabhouse Nunnery.

name: The Walks
text: Your train passes near The Walks, on the train's {side}, the football ground where King's Lynn played from their founding in 1881. A match was played there under electric lights as early as 1893, and its record crowd, 12,937, came to see an FA Cup tie against Exeter City in 1951.

name: Landwade
text: Your train passes near Landwade, on the train's {side}, once one of the smallest parishes in Suffolk: only one kilometre from north to south and at most 500 metres from east to west. In 1951 it had 38 people.

name: Clarehaven Stables
text: Your train passes near Clarehaven Stables, on the train's {side}, a Newmarket racing yard built in 1901 with a fortune won in bets on its namesake, the 1900 Cesarewitch winner. Its first stars included the filly Pretty Polly, who won 22 of her 24 races; since 2007 it has been the home of the trainer John Gosden.

name: Devil's Dyke
text: Your train passes through Devil's Dyke, an earth bank and ditch thought to be Anglo-Saxon, which runs for 11 kilometres in an almost straight line from Reach to Woodditton. It is the largest of Cambridgeshire's ancient dykes; the railway was cut through it in the 19th century.

name: Kentford
text: Your train passes near Kentford, on the train's {side}, a village on the banks of the River Kennet. In 1893 the actress Lillie Langtry bought Regal Lodge here, which she made into a grand house for weekend parties and celebrations of her racing wins.

name: The Glen Chalk Caves
text: Your train passes near the Glen Chalk Caves, on the train's {side}, 200 metres of tunnels running out from an old chalk pit with a disused lime kiln. Five species of bat hibernate in them from September to April.

name: Black Bourn Valley
text: Your train passes near Black Bourn Valley, on the train's {side}, an 88-hectare nature reserve, once Grove Farm, with the River Black Bourn running through it. Barn owls, yellowhammers and skylarks live there, and the river reportedly dried up in the drought of 2022.

name: Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket, on the train's {side}, a Grade I church of the 14th century; tree rings date the timbers of its spire to 1362 and 1363. Thomas Young, its vicar in the 17th century and the tutor of John Milton, is buried in the church.

name: Mellis
text: Your train passes Mellis, on the train's {side}, a small village with the largest area of unfenced common land in England, where Oliver Cromwell exercised his troops. The writer Roger Deakin lived at Walnut Tree Farm, on the edge of the common, from 1968 until his death in 2006.

name: Creeting St Mary Windmill
text: Your train passes near Creeting St Mary Windmill, on the train's {side}, the body of a post mill built in 1796, moved in about 1860 and used for many years as a dovecote. It is the only reused windmill body of its kind left in the country.
